slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on **Introduction to API**.
slides.image_prompt: Title Slide

slides.title: Learning Objectives Slide
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn,

• Define what an **Application Programming Interface** (**API**) is and its importance.

• Explain the role of **API keys** in authentication and access control.

• Describe how applications use **APIs** to send requests and receive **AI**-generated responses.

• Apply the analogy of an **API** as a connector between different systems.
slides.image_prompt: Learning Objectives Slide

slides.title: System Requirements Slide
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.
slides.image_prompt: System Requirements Slide

slides.title: Pre-requisite Slide
slides.narration: To follow this tutorial, you should have prior knowledge of Episode 1: Basics of Python.
slides.image_prompt: Pre-requisite Slide

slides.title: What is an API?
slides.narration:
Now, let's begin our journey into the world of **APIs**.
What exactly is an **Application Programming Interface**, or **API**?
Imagine different software applications needing to talk to each other.
How do they do it?
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: What is an API?

slides.title: Defining API
slides.narration:
An **API** is a set of rules and protocols.
These rules define how software applications can communicate.
Think of it as a menu that tells you what you can order.
And how you should order it from a restaurant.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API as a menu in a restaurant

slides.title: Why APIs are Essential
slides.narration:
Why are **APIs** so important?
They enable different software systems to connect and share data.
This allows for new functionalities and seamless integration.
Without **APIs**, many of our favorite apps wouldn't work.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing different software applications connecting and sharing data

slides.title: Common API Use Cases
slides.narration:
Let's look at some real-world examples.
When you pay online, an **API** securely handles the transaction.
Social media apps use **APIs** to share content across platforms.
Weather apps use **APIs** to get real-time weather data.
Can you think of other apps that use **APIs**?
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing icons for online payment, social media, and weather app connected by APIs

slides.title: API as a Connector
slides.narration:
With that in mind, let's explore an analogy.
Imagine an **API** as a helpful connector.
It acts like a bridge, allowing two different systems to interact.
How does this connection actually work?
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: API as a Connector

slides.title: The Request-Response Cycle
slides.narration:
This interaction involves a 'request-response' cycle.
An application sends a 'request' to the **API**.
The **API** processes this request.
Then, it sends back a 'response' to the application.
It's like asking a question and getting an answer.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a request arrow from application to API, and a response arrow from API to application

slides.title: Vague Request Analogy
slides.narration:
Let's use an analogy to understand this better.
Imagine you ask a chef, 'Make food!'
This is a very vague request, isn't it?
What kind of food would you get? It's unclear.
The chef might be confused or give you anything.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Make food!...'

slides.title: Improved Specific Request Analogy
slides.narration:
Now, what if you say, 'Make me a chicken biryani, medium spicy'?
This is a specific request with clear instructions.
The chef now knows exactly what to prepare for you.
And you will likely receive what you asked for.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Make me a chicken biryani, medium spicy...'

slides.title: Comparing Request Specificity
slides.narration:
See the difference between the two requests?
A vague request leads to an unpredictable response.
A specific request ensures you get the desired outcome.
This applies directly to how applications talk to **APIs**.
Clear instructions lead to clear results.
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague prompt output vs improved prompt output

slides.title: API Keys and Security
slides.narration:
But here's an important question.
How do **APIs** know who is sending the request?
How do they ensure only authorized users get access?
This is where **API keys** come into play.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: API Keys and Security

slides.title: What are API Keys?
slides.narration:
An **API key** is a unique identifier.
It's like a secret password for your application.
It tells the **API** who you are and that you are authorized.
Each user or application gets its own unique key.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a digital key or password icon

slides.title: Authentication and Access Control
slides.narration:
These keys are crucial for authentication.
They verify your identity to the **API**.
They also control what data and functions you can access.
This prevents unauthorized access and keeps data secure.
It's like a bouncer at a club, checking your ID.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a bouncer checking an ID at a club entrance

slides.title: Attempting Access Without a Key
slides.narration:
Let's see what happens without an **API key**.
Imagine trying to enter a restricted area without a pass.
The system would reject your entry immediately.
Similarly, an **API** request without a key will fail.
You will receive an error message.
slides.image_prompt: Screen showing an 'Access Denied' error message

slides.title: Successful Access with an API Key
slides.narration:
Now, if you provide the correct **API key**...
Your request will be authenticated.
The **API** will process it and send a valid response.
It's like showing your pass and gaining entry.
Notice the successful response you get.
slides.image_prompt: Screen showing a 'Access Granted' confirmation or successful API response

slides.title: Best Practices for API Key Management
slides.narration:
Managing your **API keys** securely is vital.
Always keep your **API keys** confidential.
Never embed them directly in client-side code.
Store them in secure environment variables instead.
This prevents unauthorized access and misuse.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, securely storing API keys, with lock icon

slides.title: Application Interaction with AI APIs
slides.narration:
Now, let's bring **AI** into the picture.
How do applications interact with **AI models**?
Specifically, how do they use **APIs** to leverage **AI**?
Imagine asking an **AI** a question and getting an answer.
slides.image_prompt: Section Header: Application Interaction with AI APIs

slides.title: Sending Requests to AI Models
slides.narration:
When sending requests to **AI APIs**,
You typically include input data and specific parameters.
For example, a prompt for a text generation **AI**.
Or an image for an image recognition **AI**.
The request needs to be structured clearly.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing an application sending input data to an AI model

slides.title: Receiving AI-Generated Responses
slides.narration:
After processing, the **AI model** sends a response.
This response is the **AI**'s generated content.
It could be text, an image, or even a prediction.
The application then uses this **AI**-generated output.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing an AI model sending a generated response (text, image) back to an application

slides.title: Simple AI Request Example
slides.narration:
Let's see a simple **AI** request example.
Imagine sending a request like, 'Tell me a joke'.
The **AI** might respond with a generic joke.
Notice the straightforward input and the simple output.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Tell me a joke...'

slides.title: Structured AI Request Example
slides.narration:
Now, consider a more structured request.
Like, 'Tell me a joke about a computer, make it short'.
Here, we've added specific parameters.
The **AI** will then generate a tailored response.
See how the output is more specific to our request.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Tell me a joke about a computer, make it short...'

slides.title: Understanding AI Response Formats
slides.narration:
**AI** responses often come in structured formats.
A common format is **JSON**, or JavaScript Object Notation.
Applications parse these formats to extract the information.
This allows the application to use the **AI**'s output effectively.
Understanding the format is key to using the response.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a JSON data structure

slides.title: Summary Slide
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined what an **API** is and its importance.
We understood the role of **API keys** for security.
We saw how applications send requests and receive **AI** responses.
And we used an analogy of an **API** as a connector.
slides.image_prompt: Summary Slide

slides.narration:

Identify how it might use an **API** to fetch weather data.
Describe the request and response in simple terms.
Compare the results.
